review:
To be completely honest, I didn't really think this game would be that good at first. I just wanted to see it through to pass some time and say that I finished yet another game, since I made it this year's goal to play some games I never touched before.

However, Shinrai made me eat my words.

Once the story *truly* picks up, Shinrai becomes an amazing story that makes you second guess the things that even you thought you knew about the game. The characters react in a somewhat-realistic way to high-stress situations, given that all of them are teenagers, and seeing how they act towards one another, given their circumstance, is really fun to see.

Again, even if the mystery itself is good, the characters are the true stars of the game. Even if they are somewhat "trope-ey", I can't say I truly disliked any of them. Their speech patterns get annoying at times, but all of them play an important role to the story at large, and you can feel that all of them know each other and have realistic relationships to one-another.

I'm not the best at this recommendation thing, but all in all, Shinrai is a great game with a good story and characters that I would very much recommend playing if you want to spend a couple hours of your weekend figuring out a mystery.

The game is a decent murder mystery that'll scratch that whodunit itch. I've seen a lot of comparisons to Danganronpa, or Ace Attorney, but I don't think Shinrai: Broken Beyond Despair is quite at that level. It feels more like a shoujo manga-esque "Murder, She Wrote" with Raiko Shinpuku taking the center stage as our sardonic protagonist. She reluctantly goes to Rie Miyamoto's Halloween party, in which a series of harmless pranks turns into the sudden death of one of their classmates. Bodies start piling up, and it's up to Raiko to figure out whodunnit before the wrong person goes to jail. The mystery itself is challenging, and requires a keen eye to skim the clues and the text in order to discern who the culprit is. 

There is one flaw to this game: Kotoba.
It's bad enough he's more perverted than Minoru Mineta from My Hero Academia. It's bad enough that he mixes languages like an american twelve year old weeb who's trying to learn japanese from poorly subbed anime. It's both traits that make Kotoba into an intolerable cringelord.
In spite of Kotoba, I am going to give this game a recommended because I did have a fun time with it.

Short but fun murder mystery game. I had a good time.

However, I do have some issues and, since I don't want to say anything about the mystery itself or the characters, this will sadly take up the majority of the text in my review:

The art might take some time to get used to but I did get used to it.
A select few tracks in the soundtrack sounded a little too messy for my taste, however.

My greatest issue with the game is the lack of an important quality of life feature. From other mystery games, I value the option to look through your evidence while prompted to answer a question (that does not involve presenting evidence itself). However, in Shinrai, when prompted to name a culprit or answer a multiple-choice question, you can not look through your evidence and notes, which I found to be pretty frustrating.

This is one of those games you can´t flatly recommend. The enjoyment you will get depends heavily on your tolerance to certains aspects of it and if you can get through the first two chapters.

The start is just bad: slow and pointless scenes, frustrating dialog, padded with anime tropes and pop culture references. The art, which is something I was worried about coming in, is actually the first thing I got used to.

After the ball starts rolling, it improves a lot. The mystery and suspense are quite well done. You always have enough information to put some things together, but not enough to get the full picture. As I was playing, I was creating and discarding my own theories in my head. The dialog improved too now that the characters were too busy to pander to their own stereotypes and had to rely on personality traits.

The ending was ok. The deductions roughly made sense, and the amount of stuff to mentally track was well balanced. It did lack a certain excitement to it. In narrative terms, it almost felt more like a catharsis than a climax.

For whatever is worth, I did end up enjoying it and look forward to future works of this dev.

Fiquei um bom tempo pensando se deveria recomendar esse jogo ou não. 

Para ser bem sincera, não é um jogo péssimo. Diria que está um pouco abaixo de medíocre. Um jogo nota 4. 

Só que existem jogos com defeitos horríveis - que têm qualidades que ao menos compensam ou fazem valer um pouco a pena. Tipo ser grátis, ser muito barato, ter uma história boa apesar de ser feio/ter uma jogabilidade estranha/ser bugado. 

Esse jogo tem defeitos em todo o espectro - de pequenos a grandes - e nenhuma qualidade grande o suficiente para salvá-lo.

1 - Trilha sonora repetitiva e pouco inspirada; 

2 - Arte...meh. Os cenários são melhores que os personagens, mas nada chega a ser lindo. Em uma VN de terror isso é um defeito significativo, porque a ambientação visual é uma das partes mais importantes do mood geral. 

3 - Ritmo bizarro. Começa com aquele monte de ladainha/besteirol típicos de anime, fica uns 30% do jogo nisso, aí morre um, morre outro, morre mais um e puf, acabou. Aí tem um epílogo com mais ladainha de anime e aparições sem nexo de personagens que nem foram mencionados na história principal. Tá, entendi que provavelmente isso referencia outro jogo da mesma desenvolvedora, mas parece o Multiverso da Loucura, é o puro caos. 

4 - Personagens: é aqui onde o jogo mais peca. O cast é simplesmente horrível. A única personagem realmente interessante é a principal (Raiko). O resto vai de sem graça a desgraça. Sabe a outra menina ali nas imagens de divulgação? Parece uma segunda protagonista ou deuteragonista né? Saiba que ela não faz nada de útil o jogo todo, só fica se escondendo apavorada atrás da Raiko. Pra não dizer que ela não tem função nenhuma, a função dela é dar álibis à protagonista e fazer a trama rodar sem os outros personagens ficarem questionando. Tem outra cuja função é ser a genki girl louca, não acrescenta absolutamente nada à trama. Os personagens masculinos são um pior que o outro (com uma única exceção) - em qualquer jogo do tipo você torce (mesmo sabendo que é em vão) para os personagens se salvarem, nesse você só consegue falar "bem feito" porque é só o esgoto. A motivação do assassino é a mais besta que já vi em qualquer VN do tipo, terminou e fiquei "ué, só isso? surtou só por isso?". Todos eles são estereótipos, o que por si só não é um demérito - Danganronpa não apenas trabalha com estereótipos como os glorifica com títulos de Ultimate, mas os personagens ali transbordam carisma, vão além do seu exterior extravagante. Aqui, tenha certeza, isso não ocorre. 

5 - História e mecânica de jogo: A maneira como os assassinatos se desenrolam é bem sacada. As áreas de investigação também, apesar de sempre simples - não dá pra dizer que tem um puzzle nesse jogo. A exploração nos ambientes escuros foi bem feita também, pena que não focaram tanto nessa parte. Senti falta de mais gente mentirosa, mais contradição, de botar a palavra de um personagem contra o outro. 

Enfim, é um jogo mediano pra ruim. Se você gostar muito do gênero e estiver SEDENTO por algo do tipo (foi assim que comprei, já joguei praticamente tudo o que existe de murder game na Terra e precisava de algo para satisfazer meu vício), vale se estiver tipo com 90% de desconto. Do contrário...tem muita coisa melhor por aí.

SHINRAI does start off a bit slow, and some players may be put off by the anime like gimmicks certain characters have. However, it's more than worth sticking with it for the central mystery and how it unfolds. It is presented in a very compelling way, one that keeps you guessing about the true culprit. I went from thinking I had it figured out, to suspecting a completely different character later on multiple times. 

As many other reviewers have already stated, the mystery is logical and very much grounded in reality. There aren't any wild jumps in plausibility or over the top revelations. Once you learn the entire truth, everything makes perfect sense. 

I really enjoy how the progression system in SHINRAI works as well. At first, accusing a character, then presenting your argument/evidence seems a bit odd. But it actually works quite well here and makes you thoroughly consider each piece of evidence, every witness account you have. I had a lot of fun with these accusation/debate sections where you go through the mystery, choosing potential culprits and then defending your accusations by presenting arguments and evidence as proof. It's a very thorough process that takes you through each part of the mystery, one step at a time. It breaks down the entire series of events and how it all happened. 

Another aspect of SHINRAI I enjoy is the characters. A few of them are a little obnoxious, maybe too much in some cases, with their respective gimmicks. However, most of the characters are likable and garner sympathy for the situation they're in. In particular, Kamen ended up being my favorite. I think Raiko is also great as the protagonist though, and while having a unique personality of her own, is often neutral enough you can feel as if you're truly solving the mystery and coming to these conclusions yourself. I appreciate all the puns throughout the game too, many of which are from Raiko. 

As I said before, the game does start off a bit slow, but I'd recommend at least staying with it for the first couple chapters. That's around the point where the game's pace starts to pick up, so I think it's a good indicator of whether you'll enjoy the game as a whole. SHINRAI is fairly reminiscent of games like the Danganronpa and Zero Escape series, so if you've enjoyed those, you'll most likely have a good time with it as well.

Short and sweet. Looking for a dark mystery that isn't going to consume countless hours like Umineko, and without the massive scale of the Zero Escape series? Something more intimate and grounded? Shinrai (meaning "trust" in Japanese) is for you.

The VN is quite short, with an intro which serves to introduce all of the characters but doesn't outstay its welcome, and then begins the wild ride that is its main plot. You are treated with the feeling that is the hallmark of a fantastic mystery story - overwhelmed, but with enough breadcrumbs to construct some idea of what is going on, only to have your assumptions challenged again and again. Eventually, you will have to construct the full truth, and while the game does poke you in the right direction, you're required to make a lot of the deductions for yourself.

The mystery itself is logical and doesn't require any absurd or unreasonable leaps of faith - it is very well crafted with lots of little details that will reward the perceptive reader. There are no Deus Ex Machinae and for those seeking an intricate and challenging but very satisfying mystery, I will happily recommend this game.

It's not without its issues - a couple of the characters feel like somewhat absurd caricatures - and I find it annoying how you cannot review your evidence once you're forced to make a decision (so if one is suddenly sprung at you, hope your memory is good!) - but overall, I'd say it's a very satisfying VN.

Also, there are lots of references to other games which adds to the fun factor - if you're able to read Japanese, you'll find some things very amusing too.

A lot of love put into this game, but it was not my cup of tea; I knew going into it that I didn't like the art style or the sound design, but I could forgive that if the writing and narrative were engrossing. I did like that it required some attention to solve the mystery, but it was not a particularly difficult mystery.  While the mystery at the heart of this story was fine, it was not interesting enough to make up for everything else.  I didn't especially care for any of the characters; the prose style (at least of the English translation) was stiff and repetitive; moments of humor were really, really bad--perhaps they simply don't translate well--and the pacing of the story was rather slow.   I could not recommend this to a lover of VNs or kinetic novels.

I remember reading Branson Reese reviews on letterboxd and there was a particular quote that stuck with me. "High school productions are often better than professional ones, because you know EVERYONE wants to be there." And that's a sentence that kept coming back to me here.

Shinrai REALLY wants to be about how lack of communication can destroy relationships. And it wants you to KNOW that's the story from beginning to end. I don't really want to be mean to an indie project, but this really feels like a game made in 2008 rather than 2016. It almost screams American middle schooler trying to write an anime, with memes and quirky archetypes and so on and so forth. Its all-encompassing and if that drives you up a tree, you're gonna have a bad time.

But I can't really work up a dislike for it.

And so I keep coming back to that Branson Reese quote. Its not always well-written or engaging, but you can really feel how much the creators cared about what they were writing. They worked really hard to write a complicated mystery, tying together different character motives so it all made sense. You can feel how they all laughed amongst themselves writing a goofy old Castlevania reference or hentai joke. Or how they committed to their protagonist wearing cat ears and had to write situations where she would keep forgetting to take them off during a murder investigation. I dunno! It was weird! It was embarrassing! It was ambitious and earnest! I had to keep skipping text because I just got overwhelmed with the sheer Middle School Energy of the dialogue. The theme is heavy-handed, but you totally buy that these are the mistakes these children were making because they didn't know how to communicate! I think I liked it a lot! Maybe!

I had more to say about this four hour murder mystery vn than the 70 hours/six months I spent on (the unquestioningly good!) Dragon Quest XI. I don't know if that's damning of me or the games, but it says SOMETHING.

[WITHOUT SPOILERS]

"HEPPY HELLOWEEN"
I think most people look to VNs trying to find wonderful stories and deep characters, and you should be aware that you will not find any of those here. HOWEVER, if you enjoy Christie, Doyle or any other whodunit AND howdunit stories, you can be sure that you will be well-served here.

It really is a fair mystery. I can see how much those two guys (yeah, just two people on the development) paid attention to details and how the story rewards you when you pay attention as well. I think the art it's fine, but even if some people are not fond of it, will you really let it prevent you from enjoying a so much well constructed plot? Just buy it! It's cheap, short, has a lot of references to other great visual novels as well, and you will probably finish it wanting to (re)watch Case Closed.
If you can tolerate some 2000s era cringe (in particular in the first couple hours), there's a decent mystery here. The ending sequence is pretty good and you will probably mess up the first time.

Right so let's begin with how I found this game. I looked up "Games Similar To Danganronpa" online and found an article with this game on the list. It looked interesting, so I decided to pick it up, and I don't regret that decision at all. This game is honestly great. 

Being a visual novel game, obviously a lot of the gameplay is reading to progress the story. There are also times where you must investigate areas in order to find evidence and clues. This gameplay is aided by a really nice UI that was extremely easy to figure out and use. 

While only clocking in at 6 hours, not the longest game in the world, those 6 hours were never wasted for a second. There was never a point where the game felt like it dragged a point on for too long, which is key in a visual novel game like this. The writing in the story is great in my opinion, despite most of the characters being based around a simple personality trait, the game can still use them well and establish a good murder mystery. Speaking of the murder mystery, I'm not going to go into that too much as to avoid spoilers, but there are no massive stretches of logic in it, nothing feels impossible to pull off in the context of the situation,  which is really nice.

The art is nice looking, while it's not the most stand out art you're going to see, it fits really well and all of the sprites are well drawn and proportionate. Same goes for the CGs which appear at key points in the story. To expand on this topic, the music is beautiful. There isn't a single track in this game that I disliked, and a couple of them I see myself listening to in my free time.

All in all, this game obviously isn't going to be everyone's cup of tea, but if you love murder mystery visual novels, this is a really great sleeper hit. I would highly recommend this game to everyone who enjoys the genre. And even if you don't enjoy visual novels that much, I would still give it a try if you can find the time. It's worth it.

I bought this game because a lot of people said it was like Phoenix Wright et al and. hoo boy. We have different standards for writing quality, I suppose.

First off, several of the characters are incredibly obnoxious to listen to and/or terrible human beings. You know, the kind of thing that is totally appropriate for a mother to think about or say to her 14 year old daughter, and was completely necessary to put in the game because (crickets)

Shortly after, you are introduced to her best friend who, in an apparent attempt to make a funny endearing sidekick a la Maya from Ace Attorney, just talks like a teenager on Gaia Online in the year 2008. She even writes out text emojis in Raiko's journal! It's Soooo Wacky!!! Here is a verbatim quote for you:

"We found a window an' let in sum moonlight, so we can see ♥♥♥♥ now! (makin' me wonder how she jotted down dat last entry in 'at darkness O_o;)"

Wow! Isn't that fun to read and listen to? Now imagine being subjected to pages of this for most of the game because she's glued to Raiko at the hip. I started skimming most of the dialogue and it made it a lot more bearable.

So you're like, okay, well, maybe that's a little obnoxious. But wait! There's a guy in here whose entire existence is to sexually harass everyone, talk about how much he wants to and/or has jerked off to them, spends all night jerking off to porno, and there's even a part where you pick up his ♥♥♥-stained pornography!! Let's not mention the part where he snuck into the room of some female students on a past school trip and put on their panties while sniffing a different girl's panties!

But they invited him and tolerate his presence in their friend group because (crickets)

And he hasn't yet been suspended from school because (crickets)

And the Good Guy character considers him his best friend and tolerates his behavior because (crickets)

He also [spoiler]stalked a girl and the good guy is like 'wow I can't believe he would have done something like that!' as if it's a mystery that the guy who constantly sexually harasses women with escalating acts of aggression could have possibly done such a thing, his other behavior was so... uh... harmless?[/spoiler]

Genuinely a lot of the dialogue is frustrating or annoying to read and often feels padded out for length. Like, you examine one thing and Nobara (your best friend) goes off on an insane tangent about it being a sci-fi cryogenic chamber or something. There is also a character who is constantly obsessed with scaring people so badly they literally pee themselves, and wants to do it to the protagonist. Like, using the words "soaked panties" and insisting she take off her underwear in public to prove it. Because that is definitely the sort of thing I want to read about a 14 year old girl and definitely the kind of normal dialogue someone would say to another person.

I'm not sure if they were supposed to be interesting, compelling characters who grow on you, but the only characters I ended up liking were Raiko and Kamen, because they (mostly) act like normal human beings.

Also - the references. Good god, the references. This game is self-indulgent in the worst way. It feels like the developers are constantly elbowing you in the ribs saying "Hey remember that one game?". A major plot point is that two of the characters dress up as twins from a horror video game... and the plot synapsis is a massive, obvious reference to a Fatal Frame game. In case you didn't get the more subtle reference, it's okay! They have a hotel room with instructions to use a camera to scare away ghosts on the wall and an ancient camera in front. Do you get it? DO- DO YOU GET IT?

No, it's okay. Maybe you never played Fatal Frame. Don't worry. There's also multiple Phoenix Wright references! Oh, and one of the characters makes a Castlevania reference that wasn't already hideously dated by the time the game released, or anything! What about a Dragon Ball reference that makes no sense? And Raiko's epilogue outfit is one massive visual reference to the iconic outfit Heather wears in Silent Hill 3!

But when you reference a piece of good media purely for the sake of "ha ha, remember that thing? we also liked that thing!", the problem is that people then remember that thing, and the things they felt playing that thing, and it causes them to directly contrast that with your own mediocre game and the feelings they are having while playing it.

So when you reference something, you expect the audience to be like "ha ha! wow! I too enjoyed that video game! What a funny and clever reference!" but instead it's just me being reminded that between Nobara saying "cray-cray" and "aw nutbunnies" every 5 seconds I could be playing an actual good video game that I enjoy.

They also shove in two cameos of completely unrelated-looking people at the very end, which I'm guessing are either dev self-inserts or supposed to be from a different game they have. Either way, not sure why they're here or why we're supposed to care about them but it sure feels masturbatory to shoehorn them in!

The thing that gets me is that there are some redeeming parts to this game. The art isn't terrible - the backgrounds are lovingly detailed, and the sprites are expressive, though the artist DESPERATELY NEEDS TO LEARN HOW TO SHADE WITH A COLOR THAT IS NOT BLACK, OH MY GOD, I'M BEGGING YOU. SHADE YELLOW WITH ORANGE. SHADE ORANGE WITH RED. SHADE BLUE WITH PURPLE. SHADE WHITE WITH BLUE. SHADE GREEN WITH BLUE AND HIGHLIGHT WITH YELLOW. The UI is a lot different from the standard Ren'py layout and there's a neat little trivia section. There's a lot of care in here.

The mystery, like I said, was genuinely interesting and at points stumping. And once they stopped irritatingly padding out every interaction, the character interactions weren't terrible. I almost walked out of it thinking it was a good game until I got hit with the epilogue with more sexual harassment from the protagonist's mother, more pointless references, and baffling cameos.

This team has definite potential, they just... need to stop being so self-indulgent, focus on getting a second writer and/or editor to focus on characterization (and do a sanity check with some of the lines - yeesh), and polish up the art a bit.

Also please don't make me ever read a line about an adult woman commenting enthusiastically on her 14 year old daughter's sex fantasies ever again, what is wrong with you, Jesus Christ

Hello Steam user who is wondering if this little visual novel is worth their time. I'm going to tell you right now that the answer is a definite yes especially if you're a mystery lover. It's also perfect for this Halloween season considering its setting.

Pros
– the story/mystery. Honestly the mystery is the best part about this game as well the characters but we'll get to that. It starts out pretty clichéd. You play as Raiko, a grumpy glasses wearing fourteen-year-old who's been dragged to a Halloween party by her best friend Nobara. Naturally it seems all fun and games until someone actually dies and it's up to Raiko to find the truth. You've seen the setup before but as with everything concept is not the be-all and end-all when it comes to quality. Even something that's clichéd can still be good as long as its execution is good. Thankfully the game takes it set up and uses it to its full advantage to give a worthwhile story that really explores the themes of trust, betrayal, and communication. I would explain more about the mystery by to do so would ruin the game so I will reframe.
– The characters. The mystery would not merely be as good is if it didn't have relatable and sympathetic characters. When you figure out the true ending it really hits home and can be quite an emotional experience when you realize the true tragedy that's at the heart of this game. The characters[spoiler]Momoko and Kamen[/spoiler]really get hit with this hard and I think I actually shed a few tears for both of them. And besides those two all the other characters from our grumpy protagonist to Mika the prankster extraordinaire all have easily memorable personalities to like, even if there's a few you probably want to bash in the head a few times but will get to him.
– The humor. Yes people die in this game and it has a pretty hard-hitting tragedy but when it wants to it can deliver some surprising laughs.
– The clue finding mechanic it's pretty simple but easy to grasp. Also prevents you from leaving a room until you found all the clues which is good because I imagine that can be frustrating when you get to the end and realize you've missed something and it be impossible to go back.

Cons
– [spoiler]Kotoba.[/spoiler]Remember how I said you would probably want to bash a few the characters heads in, he is who I'm talking about. Well... him and[spoiler]Hiro but unlike Hiro who's jackassory has plot relevance, Kotoba's[/spoiler]perverted tendencies are jacked up to eleven for no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason. He's like a poorly written Issei from high school DXD. It's fine to have him be a pervert but they could've down significantly and it would've not change a thing in the plot.
– Rie and Taiko's character designs. Okay this is probably only something that really bugs me and it's not like there's anything particularly wrong with their designs when you look at them individually, it's when you put them together that's the problem. It's very obvious from the moment she shows up on screen that Rie is head over heels for Taiko which is fine except for the fact that Taiko looks like a male version of her. I'm not kidding! When I first saw the steam trailer I thought they were brother and sister and since this is an anime inspired game... It just brings up the unfortunate thoughts. Of course they're not related in the game so there is no creepy incest ♥♥♥♥ going on but they just looks so much like each other that my brain is just screaming "NO!" Honestly it would be an easy fix just to change the coloring on one of them so they don't look as similar or give Rie a longer hairstyle so it doesn't look identical to Taiko's. Just something.
– [spoiler]Who those random characters that just showed up in the epilogue for no reason? They contributed absolutely nothing to the plot except for teasing may be a sequel. If there is not going to be a sequel for this game then they should of been removed because that's just being trollich.[/spoiler]

Neutral
– the art. Minus my gripe as mentioned above, I actually felt the art style was charming. It gave off a 90s feel which made it feel delightfully retro but I understand some people will think it's tacky having been used to newer slick looking character designs. 
– Music. Like the art gives off a distinctively retro 90s theme even know the game is set in 2010 but I thought it fit with the overall tone of the game. And honestly reminds me of the anime Detective Academy Q, a truly underrated mystery series that more people should be aware of.

As a fan of Ace Attorney and Danganronpa, I was eager to get stuck into another murder mystery game.  You play as Raiko, a somewhat emotionless protagonist who is being dragged to a Halloween party by her best friend.  As many other reviews have pointed out, the game initially starts out quite slow.  I don't see this as a bad thing per-se, but keep in mind that it will take around an hour to get to the more exciting stuff.

Oh, and that wait is [i]completely[/i] worth it.

Once the game picks up, it doesn't stop until the very end of the game.  The game will keep throwing more mysteries at you as you progress, making you question why these events are happening, and who is behind it.  Expect to end up accusing several of your classmates in your mind as you piece the puzzle together.  

You will go through a couple of investigation scenes (similar to Ace Attorney) throughout the course of the game to pick up some clues and evidence to help you find the culprit.  Speaking of, your detective skills will need to be on point in order to get the good ending.  Pick the wrong culprit, and you're heading to a bad ending.  Make sure to save somewhat frequently because if you end up with a bad ending, you'll be forced to load up a previous save file.  If you haven't saved at all, be prepared to start from the very beginning.  Thankfully the game does have an auto-skip feature that allows you to catch up pretty quickly.

My only real gripe with the game is that you will often get thrown into the evidence tab without fully knowing what exactly the game wants you to look for.  This is especially annoying if you're replaying the game using auto-skip, and then suddenly you're thrown into the evidence tab without knowing why.  There is a 'tip' button which you can use, not sure if this affects your overall rank at the end of the game though.

A lot of people have picked on the art style.  I personally don't think it's that bad, but it's obviously not at the same level of quality as Ace Attorney, Danganronpa.. etc.  The music was pretty decent too overall, especially the more unsettling tracks that play.

Overall, if you're into murder mystery visual novels like Ace Attorney and Danganronpa, I would say this one is definitely worth a look.  For a small indie team, I'd say they did a really good job with this one, and I look forward to hopefully seeing more murder mystery novels in the future from these devs.

Short version: pick this game up if you're at all into murder mystery visual novels like Danganronpa and Phoenix Wright. Don't be put off by the amateur Deviant Art look and slow beginning. The actual mystery is very well done, maybe even slightly edging out Danganronpa and Phoenix Wright by never taking any leaps in logic like those two are prone to do. You'll get a solid 7-9 hours out of this.

Long version: Let's get the two weak points out of the way first to clear away any aprehensions: the art and the beginning.

The art might make you think this was just thrown together, but it's not. A lot of work clearly went into hashing out the details of the mystery. After a while you'll get used to the art. It's serviceable.

The slow beginning. The first 90 minutes are very slow. It takes a long time for things to happen. A lot of the narration and dialogs are overly wordy. Two characters come off as painfully over the top anime trope. This is unfortunately the weakest part of the game, and I imagine it puts off some people into getting a Steam refund before the 2 hour time limit.

Just power through it. Once the murders start happening at the hour and a half mark, the game picks up and becomes engaging. Helpful advice: you can safely skim and speed read past ALL of the events before reaching the resort. I get that it's there to introduce the characters, but Danganronpa does this prior to the first murder amidst exploring the immediate mystery of how the characters got to the strange setting and exploring it. There is no such engaging aspect to the pre-murder portion of Shinrai. The whole beginning could have been cut down to half an hour.

So yeah, once the mystery kicks in, you'll be engaged throughout. There's a murder. Chaos breaks out. You're trying to piece together what could have happened, only for more chaos to break out that further complicates things. Repeat until you have a doozy of a timeline to try and work out. This easily could have been an entire chapter murder case of Danganronpa.

I do have a couple quibbles. While the events and story keep you engaged, the actual investigating feels very underused. You're introduced to the investigation mechanic during an early "tutorial" as your character pieces together clues from a harmless prank. After that, the investigation tools don't come up again until almost the very end 5 hours later.

The manner in which you point out the culprit is also a little strange. Usually these things have you start by debunking minor details, building a clear picture of what happened using evidence, then ENDING with you naming the culprit and wrapping it up with airtight evidence. Shinrai has you pointing out the culprit as literally the very first thing, then building your case from there. On one hand, I guess that's because it gives you all the clues you need to figure it out before it asks you. On the other hand, the dramatic buildup could have been better. The shock is frontloaded since you have to start by knowing who did it, then you just wind down from there explaining it to the other characters.

But whatever. You have the wrappings of an indie game with the contents of a well done murder mystery worthy of an above average Danganronpa chapter. If you liked those games or Phoenix Wright, pick this up without hesitation. Skim the text to quickly get through the first hour and a half until the murder, then enjoy.

When I first bought the game and started it up, I thought my veteran experience with Danganronpa titles and the fact I completed Danganronpa v3 without a walkthrough, alongside lackluster presentation, meant that I'd be easily able to predict how the story turned out. 

[spoiler]I should have paid more attention to lessons learned in Danganronpa. Don't trust girls with pink hair in twintails.[/spoiler]

I will start off with listing the dealkillers that might make people think twice before buying the game.
The art can be pretty ugly at times, and in the case of [spoiler]Kotoba's death[/spoiler], incredibly graphic for the style. Like, uncomfortably so. It's not bad, but coming straight off the heels of Danganronpa (and there will be frequent comparisons to Danganronpa), and often being recommended alongside it, it can make it feel a little inferior. 
The storytelling, especially in the prologue and first chapter while trying to introduce everybody but still pretty rife throughout the entire thing, suffers from a severe case of tell-don't-show; what I mean is, rather than showing us certain character traits, the writing will simply list those character traits. "This character is my best friend. She has always been there for me. Blah blah blah." "This character is a pervert who studies foreign languages." (This one done after it was already SHOWN he was a pervert studying foreign languages, mind you) It doesn't weave exposition naturally into the narrative, even though I noticed several instances where it could have done so. 
If you're right on the heels like Danganronpa like I was, don't expect Chapter 5 to hold your hand. If you expect the game to spell everything out for you like Danganronpa does - and this is both a good and bad trait in my opinion  -prepare for some bad endings.
There's an achievement for saving [spoiler]Kotoba[/spoiler], but this character really doesn't provide much motive for saving them. They're really not that likeable, so there's not much incentive except for steam achievements. [spoiler]Now if it was Mika we were trying to save...[/spoiler]

Now onto positives:
The writing is pretty good when it avoids telling us things rather than showing us. Of course, that's usually when it's trying to mislead you, such as [spoiler]at the end of Chapter 2 when everyone discovers Momoko's "body". [/spoiler] It's reminiscent of old campy horror movies translated to the visual novel genre, and it provides an interesting if somewhat familiar plot. Standard horror cliches are given some chance to be reinvented and used in a way that aids the mystery part. Like I said, when it's not rattling stuff off to be exposition-y, it's actually really solid writing. 
The mystery itself had a surprising conclusion and I did get nearly every possible road to the Bad End before I had to go look up what the answer was. For the level of writing we were getting during exposition dumps, the fact the mystery turned out so well-written is pretty surprising, and it is getting me to think about my own mystery writing as well as the earlier Danganronpa titles. [spoiler]Momoko's whole thing is pretty similar to Case 3 of Danganronpa 1, I just didn't realise at the time.[/spoiler] 
Openly queer characters was a refresher, and in proportion to reality was excellent, too. Being LGBT+ myself, seeing characters openly admit it is always good in my books, so long as they're characters first. Thankfully, [spoiler]Kamen and Kotoba[/spoiler] are. 
The music isn't as good or memorable as Danganronpa, but it's still pleasant to listen to. As in you won't be reaching to mute the soundtrack (though if you'd prefer to play Danganronpa music over the top, the options luckily allow you to turn down off the music without turning down the sound effects). 
Mika. Just Mika. Not waifu material, being 14-15 years old (can't remember which) but definitely best girl. Adorable, funny, and the only one without some connection to the events or main character. She's here for the memes and the ride and that makes her the best.

In my opinion: this game does deserve voice acting. On my channel I spent 9 hours playing this game, and I damn near wore my voice out trying to provide even lackluster casting. I'd offer my services if the game ever wants to have voice acting, but like I said, my voice acting is very lackluster.

Getting to the point: Should you buy the game?

In my opinion? Yes. There's enough here to make it well worth your while. I paid $1/hr for the experiences the game gave me, and I've spent more on experiences that don't last anywhere near as long. It is the poor man's Danganronpa, but it's not bad for the poor man's Danganronpa.

2. The music seemed to be short and loops often. Because of this, my boyfriend was getting tired of hearing one of the songs.

Despite its flaws, I'd highly suggest giving this game a try, if you're into anime, visual novels, and of course, murder mystery.

[h1]Shinrai provides a thrilling substitute for mystery fans, providing that itch of content when the well of other mystery titles dries up.[/h1]

Despite a small team of about two people, Shinrai is a rare example of an indie mystery novel delivering a surprisingly good mystery. Shinrai isn't without its flaws, but given its budget constraints, its a testament that a little passion can go a long way!

The game takes place at a secluded mountain resort, as a group of anime schoolmates convene for a Halloween party. Needless to say things go horribly wrong as murder and mayhem ensues. Piece together the clues, and discern who's truly responsible, otherwise you may wrongly send an innocent character to jail!

My initial concerns focused on the artwork. The characters possessed a flat color palette with thick black strokes, reminiscent of college Adobe Illustrator projects. The artwork certainly screamed indie; however, as a mystery novel enthusiast, I pressed on, and I'm glad I did. Once you dive into the game, the artwork morphs into something endearing, giving the characters a distinct charm. The characters adhere to basic anime tropes, but regardless, they're lovably entertaining with their expressive personalities, bad puns apenty, slapstick comedy, and playful sexual innuendo. If you've played similar anime detective games, such as Phoenix Wright and Danganronpa, you'll feel right at home.

The main character, Raiko, is the story's Sherlock. The developers make no secret she's inspired by Detective Conan with her nerdy personality, over-sized glasses, and small stature. Despite her appearance, Raiko is a surprisingly confident and mature 14-yr old protagonist who the other characters learn from, and even slowly idolize. Beneath her anti-social behavior lies a cool, calm, and collected girl, providing hilarious scenes when clashed against the game's outlandish personalities.

While Raiko makes for a good Sherlock, the same can't be said for her Watson sidekick, Nobara. Her dialog mimics a southern accent, but it comes off being hard to read. It's made worse whenever she panics, delivering stammered speech patterns, occuring frequently. It's clear Raiko and Nobara are inseparable, but in the sequel, a different Watson would be a nice change of pace, or at the very least Nobara needs to tone down the accent. A character can still have an accent without having it spelled out constantly.

None of the characters are voice acted, but that's never been a requirement for good visual novels. Bad voice acting can otherwise ruin a great game, and plenty of visual novels have stood the test of time without them. Meanwhile, the composer delivers a fantastic performance. The game could use a couple more soundtracks, as what little there is gets recycled frequently. The music is at its best in the mountain resort's creepy dark environments the characters often find themselves in, where uncertainty is in the air, and anything can jump out to surprise them. I knew the music was effective when I would brace myself for a potential jump scare!

The glaring weakness of Shinrai is its Ren'Py engine interface, suffering multiple setbacks. The game cannot be saved during decision prompts, which in the world of visual novels is unforgivable. Instead, you'll need foresight to know when important decisions approach so you can save in advance. What's worse, there's only a max of 16 save slots.

The interface panel's functionality is only available during Raiko's narration segments, so if you want to skip text, but you're stuck in a conversation, then you must progress through the conversation until seeing a narration segment to reveal the interface. The game's text also suffers persistent glitching where every few lines it gets stretched or compressed by a few pixels. You'll learn to ignore it, but it's bizarre how a visual novel engine fails to accomplish so many basic essentials.

The overall story and mystery, however, is compelling and exciting. You won't want to put the game down as it flirts with the idea of an impossible murder reminscient of an Agathe Christie novel. The player must piece together evidence acquired in various investigation segments, inspired from point-and-click games. At the game's conclusion, the player is challenged to make reason of the evidence, and declare who performed the deed. Reaching the wrong conclusion provides one of several "bad endings." Players are ranked with a final score and given various bonus content, notably hidden epilogue scenes detailing deeper motivations of certain characters.

Some players have mentioned the game takes too long to setup the introduction before it gets exciting. This is understandable, but if you're accustomed to playing longer visual novels and understand the nuisances of mystery writing, then you know exposition is par for the course. By the end of the game, you'll want to learn more about the characters anyways!

There is one flaw to the mystery that almost makes me not want to recommend the game. This is a [b]HEAVY SPOILER!...[/b]
[spoiler]According to Van Dine, "A crime must never turn out to be a suicide. To end an odyssey of sleuthing with such an anti-climax is to hoodwink the trusting and kind-hearted reader." Some of Van Dine's rules are obsolete, but this isn't one of them. The advantage of using anime as an art medium is character emotion. Shinrai doesn't give us the pleasure of fingering the culprit and watching them squirm. Instead, the reader can't help but feel the culprit accomplished their goal, escaping an interrogation and prison sentence. This is a missed opportunity for those accustomed to the precedent set by Phoenix Wright and Danganronpa.[/spoiler]

Shinrai is rather short at about 15 hours, which is a perfect length and makes it more accessible to wider audiences. Considering the game's save slot restriction, this is certainly a blessing. While it's light on content, the mystery has enough twists to keep the player guessing. It's challenging enough for veteran mystery readers, while also being a great entry point to those new to mystery or visual novel genres.

While it's hard to recommend Shinrai over bigger budget titles, such as Phoenix Wright or Danganronpa, Shinrai provides a thrilling substitute for mystery fans, providing that itch of content when the well of other mystery titles dries up. Shinrai lays the groundwork for a memorable and loving cast of characters from which the developers can build on with future titles. Raiko compares favorably to the pantheon of other mystery novel Sherlocks, and the story holds its own to even professional mysteries. There is strong potential for Raiko as a future detective star. With a sequel to Shinrai already in the works, the development team surely agrees, and it will be interesting seeing what mischief Raiko-nyan finds herself in next!

[b]Final Score: 7/10[/b]

[b]p.s.[/b] I am a mystery novel veteran who did solve the mystery on my first try with about an 86% detective rating, but only because Umineko no Naku Koro ni trained me to be a good detective; otherwise, I doubt I would have figured it out. It definitely had me challenged!

As someone who judges games a lot by their design, the art style almost made me pass on this game. I'm glad I didn't. 

Don't get me wrong, the art is not [i]awful[/i], it's just a bit too generic animesque for my taste.

That said, SHINRAI was a genuinely intriguing and clever mystery. Seemingly irrelevant details end up tying the whole riddle together. Pay attention to idle chats and what rooms characters use, as it really does matter. For me at least the mystery was hard to solve, but once it was explained, it fit together seamlessly.

As for gameplay, it was just the right amount for me. I'm a bit of a completionist, so I did balk at the first investigation event as there was a ton of things to click and examine. Thankfully, the later such events didn't require me to be so thorough. Just the right mix of visual novel and gameplay too, I'd say. 
It does however feel a bit contrived how you can't move on from an investigation unless you have found the right clues. I understand this is necessary from a gameplay perspective, but it would have been interesting in itself to let a lack of evidence lead to its own ending. Especially since you can skip through seen parts of the game pretty quickly upon a second playthrough.
   One thing I did enjoy was how the game didn't stop you from making the wrong accusation. This led me to believe I had solved it, only to be smacked in the face with a bad ending. I think it was at that point the game went from enjoyable to respectable.

I also really enjoyed how much time was dedicated to the characters. While some ended up pretty flat ([spoiler]Mika and Kotoba[/spoiler]) it did serve to create a narrative surrounding the mystery, rather then let the mystery be the end-all. That said, I had expected at least [spoiler]Mika[/spoiler] to be more fleshed out at the end, seeing as they were one of the survivors. They were probably the character who broke my immersion the most. They were simply too cartoonish in a story full of exaggerated but still [i]somewhat[/i] believable people.

And finally, a very personal note that made me extremely fond of this game. As a lesbian, I was smiling like an idiot upon solving the mystery and getting [spoiler]Kamen's[/spoiler] story. It's rare to find good LGBT+ rep in games, especially these animesque ones. Her story was relatable and uncomfortably close to home. Not only that, but [spoiler]to have a lesbian character as a main suspect, only to show that not only was she innocent, her love for another girl was the key part of the solution[/spoiler] is sadly close to groundbreaking. A lot of storytellers tend to make their LGBT+ characters the culprit, using their experiences related to their sexuality as the motivation. This often creates a tragic culprit, a sympathetic one even, but nevertheless a culprit. Queercoding your villains is a problem, and I commend this game for not falling into that trap.

In short, this game looks [i]okay[/i], but it's definitively worth the price tag. The [i]okay[/i] exterior hides a rich story. Just don't be intimidated by the very long opening.

“What had transpired here tonight was a rather complex chain of events, but I was going to explain everything as best as I could… So that they, too, would be able to understand the tragic truth behind it all. “
-Raiko Shinpuku
--------------------
SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair is a murder mystery visual novel and first in the SHINRAI series, as well as the first game developed by indie German video game developer “Gosatsu”, a duo consisting of core members Gospel and Natsu. As a visual novel, gameplay in SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair consists primarily of reading, with interactivity delegated to segments wherein the player is prompted to present evidence in order to prove or disprove character deductions. Through a series of just such segments, the player progressively pieces together the identity of an anonymous killer and reveals the truth behind an otherwise seemingly straightforward death.

A secluded mountain resort, 10 friends, 1 murderer. Investigate, interrogate and present evidence as you solve various mysteries throughout the night. Will you be able to reach the truth and uncover the culprit’s identity? Or will your deductions lead you to blame someone completely innocent…? (Steam/Itch.io synopses)
----------------

All too often is it said that “first impressions last forever” and that what defines your opinion of a person or thing is your very first, very basest of experiences with it. Quite the opposite, however, SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair establishes an identity for itself that would be somewhat unbecoming to one giving it a cursory look-over or a relatively noncommittal playthrough, and one that betrays the sheer quality of what SHINRAI eventually grows into.

SHINRAI’s introductory scene found itself, when measured against everything following it, comparatively unwelcoming: juvenile humor and a somewhat uninspired setting saved just barely by a colorful ensemble of charmingly eccentric characters. Nonetheless, as banal as it may be, it was paced expertly and fluidly presented an array of details and information that make the scene nothing short of essential.

Succeeding the opening segment, however, were a series of scenes equal parts shocking and engaging. In a number of ways, Gosatsu prove themselves masters of detail and suspense, utilizing the closed-circuit setting to create a wonderfully nonlinear mystery with a number of conclusions, all equally distinctive and convincing, bar the very truest of them, the one you’d least expect. In allowing the player to pursue any of the prospective murderers, Gosatsu creates a truly interactive murder mystery that rightly forces the player to make sense of the dizzying phantasmagoria of criminal activity they experienced throughout the night.

SHINRAI ~ Broken Beyond Despair, to the most superficial of an audience, would initially seem unappealing or generic. It is worth it, though, to read SHINRAI in its entirety, as the mystery presented rivals perhaps some of the best in the genre. Any with experience with murder mysteries and/or the visual novel genre will feel right at home with SHINRAI, as would any who just wish to read an intelligent and thoroughly thought-out story in the ilk of Ace Attorney or Danganronpa.

As a fan of the Danganronpa franchise, I figured SHINRAI would be worth a go, and it did not disappoint. The overarching mystery was well crafted, abetted by charming characters, colorful artwork, and an atmospheric sound track. On the negative side, the story is very slow to build, with key revelations and motivations unfolding in a large exposition dump at the end. Further, the writing is rather stilted at points, which wrecks player immersion a bit.

Overall, though, SHINRAI's virtues far outweigh its vices. It's an enjoyable romp, and I look forward to seeing the creators develop this world and its characters further.

I will start by saying that this review contains minor spoilers about the characters and story.

SHINRAI - Broken Beyond Despair is an indie mystery visual novel that has some elements similar to the Danganronpa series which I also am a big fan of.

The story circulates around 10 classmates that decide to hold a halloween party in a secluded mountain resort: 

Raiko - Main character. Girl that doesn't show many emotions. Appears to be unfriendly towards others
Nobara - Raiko's best friend. Laid-back personality but very gullible
Rie - Host of the party. Tends to act before she thinks. Chaotic and forgetful
Runa - Rie's best friend. Caring and kindhearted. Sophisticated
Mika - Troublemaker. Always pranking people. Goal is to scare Raiko
Momoko - Popular girl in the school. Introverted and shy
Hiro - Momoko's boyfriend. Arrogant and loves to glorify himself
Kamen - Momoko's best friend. Honest person that never holds back. Doesn't like Raiko.
Kotoba - The most hated one in the group as he's considered a creepy pervert.
Taiko - Kotoba's best friend. Kind and reliable guy. Rie's crush.

When the resort suddenly gets affected by a power outage, the 10 friends split up in groups. After the power comes back on, the friends find a dead body in one of the guest rooms. The base-story is what you would call a classic murder mystery, and is not a creative one in any way. However, just as in most murder mysteries, the characters play a very big part in the storytelling and is a crucial element in every part of the story. The characters of importance have a decent and realistic backstory which in turn also builds up the story.

Story: 6/10

The characters in SHINRAI have different personalities that are relatively realistic. However, most of them don't really stand out and they aren't really likable as characters. There weren't any conversation scenes where one of the characters did a stupid pun that was surprisingly fun, any scenes where one of the characters steps in to protect the main character, any scenes where one of the characters turns out to be a psychopath, or anything that makes them unique to the others. My favourite character was Kotoba as his perverted nature made him clearly different from the others and fun to talk to due to his stupid puns.

Characters: 5/10

The gameplay in SHINRAI is one of its stengths in my opinion. Instead of having a game where you only would read and click next, like most visual novels, the developers decided to add an investigation mode, similar to Danganronpa's. This investigation mode is a point and click mode where you investigate objects of interest, as well as talk to witnesses in order to find clues and evidence. There were also choices that you could actively pick between, resulting in several routes and results, the VN is made so that you as a player is able to deduct and think WITH the main character. The crime is interesting and complex, but it's described so that you would be able to try figure out what happened instead of just letting the main character explain everything at the end (which she later does though). The investigation mode could need some polishing and it was frustrating how you aren't able to save before making the choices.

Something that was really bothering me though, was the fact that all characters except 4 had alibis instantly and it kind of removed the suspense of trying to figure out who the culprit could be.

Gameplay: 7/10

The art is very unique to this game. It's not very polished but it's to be expected, as it was actually the developer who drew it. It was bothering me at first when playing the game as I'm used to more anime-like art like most visual novels use, but as you play the game, you'll eventually get used to it. Even though the art works relatively well for its purpose, more facial expressions could have been added as the characters tended to look the same almost always and I never saw any significant changes except for when they were crying. Though my opinion may differ from others playing the game, I'm certain that the game would have looked a lot better with anime-like art similar to danganronpa.

Art: 4/10

Even though the game had its bad points, and the fact that it was quite short a game, it was still very enjoyable to read. I had a great time trying to figure out the puzzle in my head, while changing theories left and right. As an indie game, I personally believe that they did a great job, and I would recommend it to people who love murder mysteries that allow you to think and solve the crime by yourself.

Total score: 6/10
Game was well developed mystery that allows for multiple suspects to keep deduction compelling.

A surprisingly good visual novel. Going into it I wasn't expecting too much but I feel like it was a very well done visual novel despite maybe coming off as being low budget. The mystery kept me guessing, the characters were cliche but I still liked them and the art style fit the visual novel. Overall I would recommend it, it is a little short so if you are looking for a visual novel you will get a lot of hours out of this probably isn't it.

I'd say it's kind of like playing one of the long cases of a Phoenix Wright game but with more of the darker vibes of a Danganrompa title.  If you like either/both of those, give this a shot, especially if it goes on sale.

In hindsight, this game wasn't all that great. The story was kinda weak. The characters are large stereotypical and there is a really weird gender imbalance. There are 7 girls and only 3 guys, and 2 of those 3 guys have almost no redeeming qualities whatsoever and are the two main "jerk" characters in the cast. Even the father character in the story is depicted as a bit of a creep and pervert. [spoiler] Also those 2 guys end up being the only real "victims" so basically the worst characters die and most of the good ones survive. I know it had to be this way to fit the killer's motive but it felt like there wasn't much tension to find out who the killer was, given that the ones who died all deserved it, and no "innocent" person got hurt or killed. [/spoiler]

One character [spoiler] Mika [/spoiler] is completely irrelevant to the story in that they can be removed from it and the general flow of the story really isn't affected much, if at all. A lot of the female characters also seem to be there just to fill the role of a common female archetype with the best friend archetype, the busty girl archetype etc, which results in a lot of unnecessary fanservicey scenes, the worst of which being the one at the end where [spoiler] the protagonist's female rival kisses her out of the blue. Like...what? It felt really cheesy and forced. The story ultimately felt way too focused on female fanservice scenes and emphasizing the female archetypes being displayed, while portraying the males as dislikeable and with no redeeming qualities. Even the male love interest storyline ends up amounting to nothing, without even giving him a final scene with the protagonist, who gets a kiss from the female rival instead. [/spoiler] The more I look back on it, the more I realize the story and characters were really flawed and it took a lot away from the game for me.

SHINRAI deserves your love.

As most of us do, you probably judge a book by its cover, or, in case of VNs, its art. The art in Shinrai is actually drawn by its main writer and developer and is probably not what you would call professional. However after finishing the game I think the art feels just right in context, and it doesn't hurt the joy of the story even a little bit. There are lots of sprites, lots of expressions and outfits, and a lot of characters including extras. All of them may not be AAA quality, but in this game, they definitely don't need to be. It does what it has to - you grow to like the characters and their funny quirks.

Now, onto the story. What surprised and pleased me the most is that SHINRAI is an actual fair play mystery. Which is something incredibly rare in our age of detective fiction's decline. The main "case" is not something the writer made up in three minutes and then explained with five deus ex machinaes, it's an actual well constructed fair mystery that you are challenged to solve. If you're a fan of Agatha Christie, you know what a joy this can be. There are hints, red herrings, timelines, clues, diary to keep track, suspect interviews, everything you need for your grumpy little detective kit. A must have for any serious mystery fan.
You may say that the story is nothing new and you'll be probably right. But it's an old story told in a pleasing new way, with a cast of lovely characters.

The characters are mostly well developed and written well enough to gain your sympathy and empathy. Generally I would describe them as "very cute but quite realistic". You won't hear any NYAAAA or see over the top stuff - they behave as normal people would and talk like real people do, which is something that usually separates english VNs from japanese ones. There is quite enough of good humour too.

Overall, if I had to describe the game in three words, I'd say Shinrai is: Indie, Cute, Smart.

Last of all, frankly I don't write reviews often, but in this case I believe it's justified, because Shinrai is very promising and deserves more public recognition - and the public deserves more fair play mystery VNs!

Brief Introduction: allow me to start off saying this is my first review here on Steam. The reason I decided to write one was because, at the time of writing this review, the game has been out for a little over a year but has only 25 reviews. I thought I'd contribute to that number.

Now for the game:
The game is of the Visual Novel genre, which, for those that don't know, means that it has a ♥♥♥♥ ton of dialogue with a few interactive bits thrown in. The art might seem weird at first, but I got used to it pretty fast, and I thought it looked quite decent. Like other have mentioned, the characters have a few different poses, and at some points change outfits, so it's not bad at all.

The characters are pretty anime-ish at first (which means their personalities tend to be somewhat exaggerated), but as the story progresses and you find out more about them, they can really grow on you.

The soundtrack I did find a bit lackluster though, and I kept wondering if it was a problem with my notebook, but I could always notice the music/sound effects looping, and it broke the immersion a little bit.

The story, though, is where the game does shine. Once again, like others have mentioned, the action takes a couple of hours to get started, but once it does, it's pretty easy to want to play through the game in a single session. The mystery is a very interesting one, and I found myself trying to guess what actually took place until the very end, when I had that spark in my mind and things seemed to make sense. And so, along with the protagonist and everyone else, I managed to correctly deduce the true culprit of the events that transpired. The reason I'm saying this is to show that, if you pay enough attention and keep throwing theories around your head to see what makes sense and what doesn't, it is very possible to correctly solve the mystery in your first run, as the game gives you all the tools needed to do it. The mystery in the game is very coherent (no bizarre logic leaps) and makes a lot of sense, so I think this is a huge plus.

So, for the conclusion:
-Do you enjoy visual novels/games that are like interactive books?
-Do you enjoy/not mind anime-ish characters with a somewhat exaggerated personality (that does get a bit of development)?
-Do you enjoy (actually solvable) murder mysteries?

If your answer to those questions is yes, then, by all means, give this game a go. It's very likely you'll enjoy it. If I were to rate my personal enjoyment of the game, I think I'd give it a solid 9/10, well worth it's full price.

Solid mystery style VN, the twist is actually pretty interesting and well done-- not at all what I expected, and it's a reasonable story as well. 

Definitely worth it, especially for a sale price. The only thing I wish is that there was more than just a ship tease at the end of the game for a certain yuri pairing that I won't mention to avoid spoilers, but alas...
